utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I'm Teresa McHenry. I appear here with co-counsel Mr. Giuliano Turone, and our case manager, Ms. Elles van Dusschoten. Mr. Niemann continues to be out of town and will not be here this week or next week but will be here after that. Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: May we have the defence appearances please? MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. I am Edina Residovic, defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. Mr. Delalic is co-defended by my colleague Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, Professor from Canada. MR. OLUJIC (in interpretation): I am Zjelko Olujic, defence counsel for Mr. Zdravko Mucic. In my team is my colleague Michael Greaves, attorney from the United Kingdom and Northern Ireland. MR. KARABDIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo. I am defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic. Together in my team is Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am John Ackerman. I am here representing Esad Landzo. I'm assisted by Cynthia McMurrey. May I take just a moment to raise a matter with your Honours? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At the end of our work here yesterday we were informed that there has been a new order regarding the way our clients are handled here while at the court. My client, Mr. Landzo, for instance, was put in an almost impossible situation this morning. A little tiny room that is hot, has no air, and it was very difficult for us to have any communication with him this morning. There may be a reason for that, but if there is, we were not advised that there is any recent incident that has occurred to justify these harsher measures of detention while present here at the court. We have no idea what that comes from or why it's being done, and it seems at the very least all defence counsel are entitled to be told why these harsher measures are being instituted with regard to our clients. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much. I think we'll refer the matter to the Registrar, who might be able to give an explanation as to what is happening and how to remedy it. I'm sure they will deal with it quickly. John, I think you'll take it on. Ms McHenry, I think you still have re-examination. Witness P (continued) Re-examined by MS. McHENRY

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I just have a couple of questions for him in re-examination. Then I have another issue to bring up to the court with respect to Witness P. I can do that after my -- it is probably best that I do this now. I would just ask that we go into private session for this, and, to the extent that I get to explaining to your Honours certain information that's not known to the witness, I would ask that your Honours, with respect to this, that the witness be asked if he can take off his earphones, because I don't want there to be any suggestion that somehow I have influenced him by hearing what I'm going to say. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes. It's better you complete your re-examination before going into that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Fine, your Honour. Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Take off his --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I heard the judge to indicate I should ask what is technically part of my re-examination first and then we will handle the other matters. That is how I understood your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Perhaps it is fairer not to complete these other matters with the examination itself until that were concluded and other matters which are incidental might come later.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Sir, after you were first arrested and brought to Mr. Delalic's house in the early morning hours of May 27th, can you please tell us, when Mr. Delalic talked with Dr. Ahmed Jusufbegovic, did Mr. Delalic ask him to put you to work or tell him to put you to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The tone was raised -- MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): I apologise. There is no basis for this question on the part of the prosecution. This question had been asked and answered. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Your question is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Your question is what did he say about the witness. Is that what you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: My question is on direct examination I believe the witness testified that Mr. Delalic told Mr. Jusufbegovic to put the witness to work. On cross-examination raised by Ms Residovic he, in response to a question by Ms Residovic, I think, may have given some ambiguity about whether or not -- who was asking and who was telling. To the extent there's any ambiguity, I just want to -- I'm not positive there is any, since he said what he testified to clearly on direct, but to the extent that there is, I'm trying to clarify the matter. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, both the question and the answer were clear enough and there's no basis for bringing this question again on the part of the prosecution. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think you are putting your question in the alternative, suggesting which of them, but I don't think that is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am sorry. I tried very hard to give alternatives so I wouldn't be accused of suggesting to him what the answer was. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That's what you have done. You asked him questions which could make him choose which of the things he was --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I have asked him to choose but I don't believe I have suggested the answer to him, but I am happy to reword it, if your Honours think that would be better. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: The suggestion is that the question Ms Residovic asked was ambiguous.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: On cross-examination, that is correct. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Well, it wasn't. It was very clear who was speaking to whom.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, it was very clear. Maybe I can find the transcript. It was very clear. I think there's no ambiguity at all who was speaking. Mr. Delalic was speaking with Dr. Jusufbegovic. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I think that there may be some ambiguity as to exactly what Mr. Delalic said and if he was asking or telling. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: But that was not the purpose of the cross-examination, was it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what the purpose was, but to the extent I thought there was some ambiguity, that defence counsel might argue there was some ambiguity in the record, I wanted to make sure that the record was clear. I don't think it's important. If your Honours wish -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Fine. Sir, you testified in cross-examination that there were HVO uniforms in the camp before 22nd July. During this time before 22nd July did everyone at the camp, including Mr. Landzo and Mr. Delic, wear HVO uniforms or did just some people? Can you please clarify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO uniforms were worn by Mr. Pavo Mucic, Buric Zeljko. Mr. Pavo Mucic's driver, Zjelko Buric, wore the HVO uniform and the other uniforms were the TO uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Mr. Mucic's uniform indicated he was from the HVO? Was there any insignia or how could you tell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember the insignia on Mr. Mucic's uniform but I do remember the insignia on the uniform of Buric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, in September when you went with Mr. Mucic to Mr. Delalic's apartment with the list of prisoners, did Mr. Mucic say anything to you about to whom he was going to give that list of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He said that he was taking it to the archive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Your Honour, that completes my questions in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Direct -- re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: In re-examination. Thank you, your Honours. I have another matter that may involve this witness, and I wish to find out how your Honours wish to handle it. I would wish to ask that in private session, and I think it would probably be appropriate, so there's no suggestion that I've influenced the witness, that the witness be asked to take off his microphone -- his headphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know whether this witness speaks any English at all or not, but if there's going to be some discussion, it's pretty conceivable that one of the two lawyers from ex-Yugoslavia may be saying something and they will be definitely speaking in a language I can understand without an interpreter. It may be more appropriate if he left the room for a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That's a fair point. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think so. If it concerns him, he doesn't have to be here. When we take a decision about him, he will know what the decision is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Fine, your Honours. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: If he has concluded his evidence, he can be discharged.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: He has concluded his evidence concerning the questions he was asked thus far. I would certainly notify the court that the prosecution may be seeking to recall him for other purposes other than directly what he has testified to, and that's what I wanted to bring up with the court, to find out whether or not the court wished in the interest of economy and efficiency and getting some of this information out, which may be directly relevant to things your Honours are hearing now, or whether or not you wish to seek -- whether or not you wish us to recall him at a later time. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Definitely if he has concluded his evidence in respect of what he has been invited to, that is all for the time being. If there is any intention to have him for some other thing, then that application is a different one and we have to take it into account, but not in his presence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Fine. I would ask that he be excused and that I be permitted to address your Honours briefly in private session. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. P. You are discharged for the time being. If the prosecution wants you for another thing, they'll get in touch with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I am not going to put words in Ms. McHenry's mouth but it might be appropriate to ask him to wait in the witness room, have a cup of coffee, wait for fifteen minutes. Would that be something the prosecution accepts as a suggestion. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That depends on the way the prosecution organises themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The prosecution welcomes that suggestion. (Witness withdrew from court) (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: (In open session) (Witness enters court) MIRKO DORDIC (continued) Examined by MR. TURONE JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Will you kindly tell the witness he is still on his oath?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I should like to remind you that you are still testifying under oath. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Mr. Turone, you can start.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Good morning, Mr. Dordic. Yesterday we were talking about your first arrival in Celebici and description of conditions of life in Hangar 6. Now I would go back to your assertion about your possession of a weapon and my question is: was there a time while you were in Celebici when you were requested to hand over this weapon or any weapon you might have been -- might have had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (In interpretation): good morning. I should like to continue. A few days after I was brought to Celebici the guards called me, and when I came out of the hangar Guska Jasmin was waiting for me, who was, I think, secretary of MUP, Sevko Niksic, who was the Commander in the police station, and Sadik Dzumhur, known as Diksa, who before the war was the director of a military training centre belonging to the Territorial Defence in Borci. Borci is a Serb village, which was then under the control of Serbian forces -- of the Serb people, I mean. They asked me -- Diksa shook hands with me and asked me how I was. I said: "You can see how." Then he asked me: "Do you know where Rajko is?" I said I did not. He told me he had been arrested and that he was in Number 9. He asked me whether I wanted to see him. I said: "No", because I thought that was just a trick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is not a question you asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you explain who is Rajko?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is not the question you asked about the weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I imagine he is going there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You have to direct him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you please be more responsive to my question? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Repeat your question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ask him a straight question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: My question is: was there a time while you were in Celebici when you were requested to hand over your weapon or your weapons, if any. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Limit your answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm telling you in the order things happened. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: No. You were asked about weapons and what you said --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: You don't have to go that far back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You are invited to arrive anyway to the answer of that question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You see, he told us yesterday that he had an automatic rifle which he left at home before going out to take protection in some Serbian area. So you asked him: "In the camp somebody asked you to surrender the weapon?" Let him say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I believe the witness understood my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood and in that conversation Jasmin Guska asked me: "Did you have a gun?" I said I did. He asked me: "Where is it? Did you surrender it?" I said: "No, I had it near the house", because Jasmin Guska was a vet for some time. I had cattle and he would visit often. He knew where my house was. I explained where the rifle was. Then he asked me: "Would you come with me so that we can bring it?" I said: "Yes". He said: "Okay. I'll send somebody to take you there." After some time I went in the hangar. They went away. Then they called me again. There were three policemen: Vahid Alagic; somebody called Sljivo -- he was a goal keeper in the Igman soccer team -- and another one, another policeman, whom I knew by sight but I didn't know his name. We sat in a police car, a Golf, and we headed for Bradina. The policeman I didn't know and Sljivo kept insulting me, saying how I stank, how all Cetniks stink, and then this other one warned them not to behave like that way. My hands were tied behind my back. I was sitting on the back seat. We got to my house, if I may put it that way. When I came out I saw that everything was burnt down; so what used to be my house. My mother was in front of it. She was about 70. Sljivo started beating me. Vahid had told him not to, because my mother was watching me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, please. My understanding of the question was: "Were you required to surrender your weapon?" It seems to me the obvious answer to that is "yes". If it always takes this long to say "yes", we may be here three or four days. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Actually they were going to collect the weapon. I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's too long. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That is a familiar pattern in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I wanted to ask him how did that happen. He is answering. May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ask him whether they were able to recover the weapon or not.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ask him whether they were able to recover the weapon or not. That is simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How did it happen that you -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Did you recover the weapon when you went with them?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: This is exactly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ask him to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you recover the weapon and hand that weapon over? This is what he is actually answering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He is not answering that. He is giving an --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm telling you how this happened, how I recovered the weapon. Vahid asked me where it was and I explained where it was. He said: "Do you know the number of the rifle?" I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object at this time that it is still unresponsive both to the question Mr. Turone asked and the question that Judge Jan asked, which is a fairly simple question: "Was it recovered?" This is like asking somebody what time it is and he tells you how to make a watch. As Judge Karibi Whyte said, it is a familiar pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I respond to that? I would invite the witness to be a little bit faster in arriving to the point, but anyway we cannot prevent the witness, I believe, your Honour, from giving his account of his experiences as he recalls them anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure you can. You can ask -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That's where we want the experience. You did not want the experience in this case. What you wanted was whether he was asked about a weapon. He said he was. Now whether he now recovered the weapon and gave them to them -- gave the weapon to them. He did. I suppose that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Exactly, your Honour. So did you hand the weapon over to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had just got to that spot when we found the weapon. I showed them where it was. The policemen jumped over a fence. Before they asked me what the number of my rifle was I told them. They looked at the rifle. They checked and they knew it was mine by the number. They checked to see whether I had fired from it. It was clean, so they confirmed that I hadn't fired a single bullet. We got back into the car and they took me back to Celebici, to Number 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So apart from this episode, were you interrogated by military investigators while you were in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About ten days later an interrogation occurred. They called us in groups of five, six, sometimes ten. A soldier would come with a list, calling out the names of people who had to make statements. There were five or six of us in my group. I don't exactly remember all the names. We were taken to the command building of the camp. We were lined up against the wall, facing the wall, and we had to stand like this (indicating), with our arms raised, and to show two fingers in a V-sign. One of the soldiers would call out people one by one to go to the interrogation room. It still wasn't my turn. Somebody patted me on the shoulder. I turned around and this person said: "Hello" to me. It was Nusret Sacibovic, who used to work with me. He worked in the same company as I. He was a lawyer there. But here he acted as a military investigator. He told me: "Mrki, be careful what you say. This is an important list and you are on it." When my turn came, I entered the office. When you go in it was to the left. When I went in, I saw Miro Stenek, somebody called Tomic, whom I knew. He was a teacher, and a typist, Ismeta. I don't remember her surname.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, where were you treated before the interrogation, while you were waiting for your turn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was facing the wall with my hands raised against the command building outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So when you entered the room and you saw -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That was not your question. Your question was: where was he treated? That was your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Is there anything else to say about how you were treated waiting your turn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't see who it was, but the military men were provoking people, saying things, but there was no beatings, at least not in my group. They were just saying nasty things and cursing us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. After entering the room where Stenek, Tomic and Ismeta were, did you see any of these people in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were you treated during this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correctly, at least as I was concerned, because Stenek knew me personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this interrogation were you in a position to face the window of the room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what could you see through that window?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could see soldiers walking around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the interrogation were you accused of anything specific?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They kept accusing me. I said what I knew. Some of the things I denied. At one point Stenek even offered me a cigarette. I had one and then he said: "Go on talking", that he was sure that I was speaking the truth. Then they asked me whether I was a member of the SDS, that is the Serbian Democratic Party. I said I wasn't and I indeed was not. Then they asked me many other things, how the weapons had reached us, whether there was any military organisation in Bradina, and that sort of thing, where I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you sign any piece of paper after the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did. I signed a statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that a long interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it wasn't very long, in my case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they interrogate you again about your weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, later on, during my stay in the camp, individual guards, if that is how I can call them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean during this interrogation were you interrogated --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Yes, they asked me about weapons. They spoke mostly about weapons. During the interrogation they spoke most about weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give them any answer to this issue, concerning this issue of weapons during the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you tell them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They asked me how I had got my weapon. I told them I had bought it and that sort of thing, on the black market.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any judicial proceedings against you after this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but for some others there was at the end, in the course of 1994. For some of the inmates who stayed until the end, until the exchange, some criminal proceedings were initiated. One of the detainees was sentenced to 12 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this interrogation have any other legal consequence concerning your position? Did they take any decision concerning you after this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll object to that question unless it can be shown that this witness is somehow an expert on what legal -- or has some feel for what legal consequences were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I do not think this is an appropriate question. He wants to find out whether he was prosecuted on the basis of his statement or not. He just wants to find out -- not the legal consequences in the abstract sense -- he means: was he prosecuted on the basis of his statement or not?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is what he wants to find out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were put into groups that they only knew what they were about. There were several categories, first, second, third. Then we learned through the guards and through Ismeta which category we had been placed into, which category of detainees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get to know in which category you were classified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was put into the first category, as one of the worst.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And this was confirmed later, because I was among the last group of 32 people to leave the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dordic, you can see a model in front of you. Can you understand what does this model represent? You can stand up, if you wish. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: You can stand up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You can even turn around the table, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the former barracks of the Yugoslav People's Army, which was later transformed into the Celebici camp when we were brought there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to provide the witness with something to point, and I would like you, please, to indicate in this model the places you have been talking about already. I believe the court will allow you to turn around the table, if you feel better so doing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Will you be able to hear me? This was the entry to the former barracks, later the camp and women were put there (pointing). My sister and some other relatives were here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can't hear very well. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. They cannot hear you, because your microphone is too far away.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the entrance to the former barracks. This was the reception where women were accommodated, detained women. Among those women was my sister and my brother's wife. This was the command building (pointing). These were some dormitories and warehouses and some toilets, and this was the building known as the infirmary, Number 22. This was the road leading there (pointing) to where I stayed, to the hangar. This was a water tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. Can he identify that building? He is saying: "This is this". The transcript is not clear what he is identifying. Each of those buildings has a number or letter on top of it. If he could say: "A was the administration building", I think that might make the record clearer and a whole lot easier to read at some future date, which is something I think we are all going to have to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Can you please say what is on the sticker of the several buildings you have been recognising, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Pointing), A is the reception, where the women were. B is the command building. D is a warehouse, a dormitory and some toilets and things. E is Number 6. This was a warehouse. There was somebody called Kernic. That's number F. They were repairing weapons there. Here again there were some warehouses I knew. We unloaded certain goods that were coming here to these warehouses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That might be enough.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We unloaded weapons here two or three times. I participated in unloading weapons somewhere in June and July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mirko Dordic, you can --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me just add there was a machine-gun nest here (indicating) and a bunker was over here that some detainees had to dig for the guard Landzo. This is where we went to urinate, to piss -- I'm sorry -- and this is a hole (indicating) that was dug that we used as the toilet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dordic. You can sit down again. So, Mr. Dordic, did you personally suffer any other physical maltreatment during your stay in Celebici besides the beating on the very first day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. That's a longish story.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean -- did that happen once or more than once?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That happened several times. The first time it was somewhere --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe in detail one by one every single incident, if possible in chronological order? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first beating that I experienced down there was when I was brought out by the guard Landzo and Mr.dzic Kemal and some name called Salko that was also waiting there. I know his first name was Salko. They brought me to this hangar number -- letter F. They put me against a wall and they asked me about some grenade, some pistols, and I had no answer for that. They kept kicking me but that didn't last long and then they returned me to the hangar. After a while on one occasion Delic came in, followed by Landzo. They walked around. They looked all prisoners over. We were all looking down with our legs pulled up. At one point they came to me and they said: "You", and ordered me to come out. Zenga took me out. He had a stick in his hand and later on I found out it was a baseball bat, because I had not seen it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Who had that baseball bat? There were two persons, Landzo and Delic. Who had the baseball bat? There were persons, Landzo and Delic. Who had the baseball bat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The baseball bat, Landzo. He brought me outside and brought me to hangar letter F. He lent me against the wall. I was leaning against it, facing it (indicating) and leaning with my hands and then he put a piece of metal in my mouth so that I could not be heard, that I would not utter noises, and he started beating me on the legs and in the ribcage. He kept asking about a machine-gun. It went on for a long time. I think he was asking for this machine-gun, I think M-53. I didn't know about it but there was a man later who knew where this machine-gun was. So he kept insisting to me to tell him where it was. He kept beating me. I fell down several times, losing consciousness. He would raise me again and continue to beat me. When he had had enough -- well, that took a long time -- I could barely get back to the hangar. The prisoner next to me, Jovan Kuljanin, he said he was counting the blows and I had received over 200 of them, up to 250. I was all black and blue so that after a period of time following that I was immobile. I could not get up. They had to help me. I had water and I would put some water on my pants, on my calves, so that the swelling would subside somewhat, so that these haematomas, these bruises, would go away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you say approximately when did this incident happen, at least in which month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this was in June, end of June, the second part of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Then can you describe then any further incidents you suffered personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was constantly a victim of Zenga's. Every time he would walk into the hangar, when he would walk from prisoner to prisoner, he would come to me and he would order me to get up and do push-ups. He would count and as he was counting, he would kick me in my ribs. So I would have to do ten push-ups. I would have to do 50 of them in order to get ten correct ones according to him. He kept kicking me all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Landzo say anything in doing that to you usually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rarely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't get the translation of this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Rarely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rarely. Rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say then anything about any further incident you suffered personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My next -- how shall I put it -- duel with Landzo was some time in mid-July. He came to the spot where I was. He had me get up and said to other prisoners: "You'll see what's going to be left of him". I thought that he was going to kill me, but he brought me to the door. We did not go out. He just brought me to the corner there, and he ordered me to kneel down. I knelt down. He poured gasoline. I saw there was a bottle for the lighter. He had pincers and he started heating these pincers. He asked me: "Where's Mico?" I didn't know at that time what Mico he was referring to. Only later I understood who it was and I told him that I didn't know. When he heated these pincers enough, he started -- he ordered me to open my mouth, to stick out my tongue, and then he started squeezing it on my tongue (indicating). He started burning my tongue. It was like being grilled. Then on the nose, and then at one point he went into the ear. He stuck the pincers and I felt a great pain and I screamed. I realised -- and something started rumbling in my head, and all this was observed by one of the guards. I think it was Salko, and he said: "Here comes Pavo". He ordered me to go back to my place immediately and he ran out. Later some prisoners -- one of them got some yoghurt and one of them gave it to me so that I would alleviate my pain and also the temperature. It took at least a month before all this was healed. Only about 20 days later did I -- was I allowed to go and be examined, and this was after Zenga was removed from the camp. He was chased from the camp. I think Pavo did that. There was a visit by Dr. Relja Mrkajic and Petko Grubac. After their intervention I was taken to the infirmary. I had pus coming out of my ear all the time. Relja told me at that time and he said my ear drum had been ruptured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there any other episode, any other incident you suffered personally you can remember and describe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were these collective beatings. These collective beatings -- now this was just the row that I was in. Somebody was talking a bit louder and Delic came in the door and asked then a Cecez whom he had appointed as sort of like room leader. He said: "Who is making noise here?" He sort of just pointed to our row. He had a baseball bat in his hand. He ordered us to get up, facing the wall, and he beat us. I don't know how many times he beat everyone. He hit me twice. After these collective beatings there were others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Dordic. Did Mr. Delic say anything in doing that, in beating you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go ahead to the next incident.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next collective beating was following 12th July. Later we found out that on that day --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Dordic. By the way, when approximately did the first collective beating you just said take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some time in early July, early in July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next collective beating was immediately following the 12th, so that was on 13th July, and later we found out that a group of Muslim police in Bradina was killed. There was a duel among them, and then they tried to blame all this on us. So we had several collective beatings. It was mostly done by Delic. When he would get tired, someone else would take over, either Landzo or Kemal Bendzic or another one whose nickname was Focak -- we didn't know his name -- or some others. These collective beatings went on for a very long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any other incident after this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next collective beating was after the visit of the International Red Cross. The International Red Cross came to us in August -- I think it was 12th August -- and delegates -- the representatives of the Red Cross entered the hangar and instructed the guards to get out, but they probably were listening to what we were saying. The Red Cross registered us at that time. They distributed cards that we filled out, and that was a sign of registration. They asked about conditions. We talked about the behaviour of the guards. After their departure, and it was close to dusk, at one point Delic came in with a group of -- I'd say 12 soldiers. He split them into two groups and ordered the ones against the wall to face it, to sit down and put hands like this (indicating). Then kicking started, so to speak. All the guards went one by one and everybody was kicked several times. I think I received about 20 blows to my kidney area at that time, and Delic was then commanding, and he had some favourites, and he would say: "Pass this one over." So these would be passed over. After it was done, he ordered: "Turn around." We did and they left the room. They left the hangar, that is. The next collective beating was some time in September, when they found playing cards which we -- makeshift playing cards which we had made out of cardboard to pass the time. Delic and some other guards beat us at that time with shovel handles and other tools, and that also went on for a long time, and we were all beaten. In the end I was brought out together with a few others. I don't know the names. I know that one of them was Damjan Dordic. He brought us out of the hangar. He put us against a wall and he ordered some guards to beat us. I saw that I was being beaten by Seki -- that's his nickname and last name Pajic. He said: "Sorry, buddy", because, you know, we were good friends. He said: "I'll beat you lightly." However, one of the guards, Zajko Camdzic said: "What are you stroking him for?", and Zajko Camdzic, he beat me with a plank which was 10 by 5 cm., which was used to prop the door. So at that moment -- how shall I put it -- I relieved myself in my pants, and I said: "Well, I'm finished now. Beat me." Then he said: "Look, the Cetnik has shat". Then he ordered someone to bring water for me to wash up and I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say: "He said: 'Look ...'", etc., who is the person you are talking about when you say "he"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Delic, about me, because at that time I had relieved myself in my pants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any other incident concerning you personally during the period of your stay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next incident was after another visit by the Red Cross. I guess the International Red Cross ordered of them or requested of them when there was only a small group of prisoners that remained to put up beds for us, and when they were doing that, then there was another beating, and Delic brought me out at that time and beat me together with another group of about ten prisoners. They were kicking us in the kidney area and in the crotch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say approximately when did this happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was some time in October. I'm not sure but I think it was in October. I'd say late October. Either late October or early November, somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any other incident you suffered personally, or was this the last --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The last collective beating took place on 1st December, when we had already been moved to Number 22. This group of 32 prisoners. This was during the day, and Delic walked in. He had a note or a letter, and he was looking for Miroslav Boric. He asked him: "Is your wife's name Zora?", and he started reading it, from his letter that his wife Zora in the village of Kukrice is looting Muslim houses and is taunting Muslims. I don't know where this letter had come from. So he took Miroslav Boric out and we heard terrible blows. He was beaten for a while. I did not see by whom, because the door was closed. After a while they shoved him back into the hangar. Then he called -- there was a guard. His nickname was Crni. I think his name was Nermin. He was from the Doboj area. He started selecting particular prisoners and then we heard them -- brought them out. We heard them being beaten. We couldn't see. The door was closed. At one point he came in and he said: "All the ones who had been captured in Ljuta near Kalinovik have to come out." There was a group of prisoners who had been captured there. So out of those 32 it was only four of us who were not beaten and I was one of those lucky ones. This was just before his arrest. He was arrested on 2nd December. We learned that from some guards. That was the happiest news for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, Mr. Dordic. Did you personally during your stay see any mistreatment of any other prisoners, specific mistreatments of any other prisoners while you were in Hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw quite a bit of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would you please describe in detail the incidents you observed personally one by one, and can you describe them in detail and possibly in chronological order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can recall certain things in order and some others I may not. I can start in order. You know, you try to forget these things anyway. Let's begin, for instance, with Mrkajic Vukasin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This Mrkajic Vukasin was one of the prisoners that was really tortured a lot. He was always suffering blows especially by Hazim Delic. He would always hit him, almost every time he would come to the hangar. He would at least get a kick or two in the kidney area. Landzo also did the same. On one occasion Landzo tied -- what is it -- a slow-burning fuse around his waist, around the genitals and stuck a piece in his anus, and then he lit the other side, and ordered him to run around, and he did, and when he -- when it reached the end, he started dancing around, and later he let him go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, can you say approximately when did this incident happen to Vukasin Mrkajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in July. I think it was late July or mid-July, somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that happen inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, inside the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you personally see the person putting fire on the fuse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Landzo, Mr. Landzo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the fuse -- was the fuse wrapped around the body of Vukasin Mrkajic while he had dresses -- trousers on or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He took off the trousers and he wrapped it around his bare skin and then after it was wrapped up, he ordered him to put the trousers back on and only one piece would stick out that he would light.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Dordic. Any other incident you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did the same thing to Risto Vukalo, the same thing with the fuse, same case. He would wrap it around his waist. He would light it in the same manner and he would run around until it was all burnt out. Also Risto Vukalo had to do push-ups, just as I had to, very frequently. He would do push-ups and he would kick him in the ribcage. Once he even beat him with a folded military belt and he ordered him to lie down on the stomach and his back was -- his bare -- he had ordered him to take off his tee shirt and he was beating him on the bare back, and all this was happening inside the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the incident with the fuse concerning Risto Vukalo take place the same day as the one concerning Vukasin Mrkajic or on different days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Different days, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The mistreatment was done by the same person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Landzo, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can you now describe any further incident concerning other prisoners you might have eyewitnessed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next incident, also with a fuse, was on prisoner Vaso Dordic. He did the same thing, ordered him to pull down the pants. He wrapped fuse around his waist, around his genitals and put -- stuck the end in the anus, and then he had to put on trousers again, and he lit the fuse, and he had to run around until it was burnt out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, can you say approximately when did this incident take place, the one concerning Vaso Dordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some time in July, because he was brought in -- Vaso Dordic was brought in to Celebici camp on 12th July in the evening, at night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Did you -- did these three people receive any medical care after these incidents, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Landzo say anything doing all this to these people during these incidents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was saying something to Vaso but I don't know what. I was far away. At the time when he was doing it, he was telling him something but I don't know what it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right then. Is there any other incident concerning other prisoners you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For instance, two brothers, Veso and Vaso Dordic, on one occasion -- Zenga abused them badly inside and outside of the hangar. Once he entered the hangar, ordered them both to get up. They did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "he entered the hangar", who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean Landzo. I'm talking about Landzo. He entered the hangar. He ordered these two brothers to get up. They got up. They stepped aside. I don't know who he ordered first to kneel down. He ordered the other one to take off the pants and then he ordered him to put his genital in the mouth. That went on for a couple of moments, I don't know how long. Then he switched them, so that the other brother was doing the same thing. He laughed at that and he was telling them something. That was Zenga. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think we will break now and come back at 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. (11.30 am) (Short break) (12.00 noon) JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Mr. Turone, you can carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. So, Mr. Dordic, you were talking about an incident concerning Vaso and Veseljko Dordic. Can you say -- the oral sex incident. Can you say where exactly did that happen inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just in front of where they were sitting, almost right next to the entrance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear Mr. Landzo saying anything during this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was laughing and saying something, but I didn't understand what.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So is there any other incident concerning other prisoners you might have eyewitnessed personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was, with Dusko Bendjo. He also suffered from Zenga. Zenga humiliated him terribly within the hangar and outside it. In the hangar Zenga would burn Dusko Bendjo. He would force him -- no, not burn him, sorry -- he would force him to do push-ups while he was hitting him in his ribs. Then he called him out once, took him outside, and after some time when Zenga brought Dusko Bendjo back into the hangar, his trousers were on fire. One leg -- I think it was one trouser leg, his right one, I think. Zenga was standing at the door and he said that no-one may extinguish it. He sat down and the trousers burnt until they were extinguished of their own. When Zenga left, his brother, Dusko's brother, and some others took off his trousers, what was left of them, and they saw large burns, wounds on his legs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are getting to a point where he is starting to talk about what other people heard and saw. He's not testified that he saw any burns or wounds, but he says: "They saw." I would just like the court to remind him that he is permitted to talk about what he saw, and if the prosecution wants to introduce what someone else said they saw, then they have to go through the proper foundation. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Ask him whether he saw the instances he is describing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, did you personally see the leg of Mr. Bendjo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because he was about 6 to 7 metres away from me -- in fact, even less than that, because his position where he sat was not very far from me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was just across the way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So could you personally observe details of how this leg appeared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe this leg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were big blisters, so big (indicating), on his leg from his thighs right down to the lower leg on the front side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Dordic. So is there any other incident concerning a prisoner, another prisoner, you could eyewitness yourself in part or in all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion Zenga -- actually, he was constantly taunting and beating Nedjelko Draganic. On one occasion he took him out, and when Nedjelko returned, we saw that -- I think it was his left trouser leg that had been burnt as far as the knee almost, and on the lower leg we saw a big wound, a big blister of this size. He was maybe 3 metres away from me, maybe even less. He told me that Zenga had poured him with gasoline.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. I asked a moment ago that the witness be instructed not to testify what other people told him. I wish the prosecution would be more careful with that and at least establish the proper foundation who it was who told him and whether or not reliability can be established for that. That's my objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I respond, your Honour? The witness is describing what he saw with his eyes concerning the leg of Mr. Nedjelko Draganic. So my question is: could you see personally the leg of Mr. Draganic when he came back into the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I also watched him for the next month at least, because he was 2 or 3 metres away from me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Did Mr. Nedjelko Draganic and Mr. Dusan Bendjo receive any medical care after these incidents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This prisoner, prisoner Bendjo, maybe after some time we treated him ourselves with primitive ways. One of the prisoners had some toothpaste on him, and he put it over his wounds, over the blisters, which burst later on, so these wounds took a long time to heal. Nedjelko Draganic, not straightaway, but a couple of days later was taken to the doctors. They cleaned it up, I suppose -- I don't know what -- because the wound had become infected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again about Mr. Draganic, right after he returned to the hangar, did Mr. Draganic say immediately what had happened to him outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he told us immediately, and we saw anyway that his leg had been burnt, that he had -- and he told us that it was Zenga who had done it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Any other incident concerning other mistreatments to other prisoners inside Hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion Zenga came through the door and he stopped in front of Momir Kuljanin's place. He took him out. I don't know what he did to him, but when Momir Kuljanin came back, he had a terrible blister on his hand this size (indicating). This was 5 or 6 metres from me. I can show you where he sat. He told us that Zenga had heated a knife on a flame and that he had forced him to hold that knife with his hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Momir Kuljanin receive any medical care after this incident, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally eyewitness, observe any other mistreatment besides what you said so far?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a lot of that. I could start telling you about it. Each time Hazim Delic entered the hangar, because he came as a big boss -- he always had two pistols at his belt. Sometimes he was wearing a camouflage uniform, sometimes in black. He often came with a gun with his fingers on the trigger. On one occasion he was holding the gun up. He fired. The bullet hit the roof. It splintered, and on that occasion a piece of the bullet hit Davor Kuljanin on the forehead, Branko Mladic on his finger, and Momcilo Mrkajic somewhere here in the neck. He took them out immediately to the infirmary, to the doctor. They took out the shrapnel. I didn't see it, but that's what I was told. The shards were taken out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you observe any other incident concerning other prisoners while you were in Hangar 6 besides all this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whenever he came to the hangar --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. When you say "he came", who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whenever Delic entered the hangar, and he would come five or six times a day -- I'm talking about Delic -- he would come five or six times a day, and almost every time he would pick out Nedjelko Samoukovic because he was next to the wall. He would order him to turn around and he would hit him with his legs. He would kick him, or with a baseball bat in the kidney area and in the genitals. He would do this almost on a daily basis until Nedjelko was transferred somewhere in July to Number 9, as they called the popular tunnel. Later when he was brought back from Number 9, when Nedjelko Samoukovic was transferred on 31st August again, then Delic continued to do that almost on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this all you can say about mistreatments of other prisoners, or is there any other incident you might describe without entering into the issues concerning people who died, I mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were daily incidents. Principally, on one occasion Landzo came in. He was walking from one prisoner to the next and he reached the position of Milivoj Gligorevic. This was 2 metres or 1.5 metres away from me. He made -- he ordered him to turn around to face the wall in his sitting position. He took a shoe and ordered Boro Koprivica to hit him with the shoe on the body. Boro Koprivica, when he was arrested, suffered terrible injuries, so that he was off-balance. He started hitting him lightly, and then he ordered him to hit him much harder. He took the shoe away from him and showed him how he should hit him and then he did. After some time he ordered them to stop. There were other such cases. For instance, Zenga once reached a father and son, Danilo and Miso Kuljanin. He ordered them to get up and start hitting each other. At first they did it lightly. Then he ordered them to do it harder, and so they had to do as Zenga told them. So this went on for some ten minutes, this mutual beating. Then Zenga, Landzo, did the same with two brothers, Vaso and Veso. All this was happening inside the hangar. He also ordered them to get up and slap each other, which they did. Mutual slapping ordered by Zenga had to be done by two cousins, Momir Mrkajic and Goran Mrkajic. This same kind of slapping upon Zenga's orders was carried out by Kuljanin Branislav and somebody called Ristic, whose first name I cannot recall, and there were other such instances. Once Landzo Zenga ordered Dragan Gligorevic to hit individual prisoners, which he refused to do, because he said: "You can hit me, but I won't do that."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, do you know now anything because of your direct knowledge about the circumstances of the death of any prisoner inside the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know quite a bit about it. For instance, regarding the death of Miso Kuljanin I think that was the Muslim holiday, Kurban Bajram, and they were looking for a victim. Zenga came through the door and called out for a volunteer. As Miso Kuljanin was known as the volunteer, he got up and went out. After a few minutes we heard a shot. Three prisoners --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A couple of minutes later three prisoners who were using the toilet outside and they ran in and showed us with their fingers --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Wait a minute. Maybe it's better you follow my question. So you said you heard a shot coming from outside; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After how long did you hear the shot from outside after Milorad Kuljanin going outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could have been two or three minutes later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately at what time of the day did that happen? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere in the morning, before noon. We didn't have a watch, so we could tell the time by the weather.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you have any chance to see Mico Kuljanin again after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you know, was there any other prisoner from Hangar 6 outside at the time you heard the shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were three prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you personally know these three people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Momir Mrkajic, Janko Glogovaz and Zjelko Cecez, known as the Spaniard, who was killed that same day, only in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These three people were prisoners as you, detained in Hangar 6; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these three prisoners come back into the hangar after the shot you heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They ran in and they showed us with their hand as if a trigger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, please, Mr. Dordic. Did they come back into the hangar together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All three of them together, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long after the shot did they come back together into the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A couple of seconds, maybe a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did these three people do right after coming into the hangar again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They showed us with their fingers that he had been killed, that he had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Janko Glogovaz, or Momir Mrkajic, or Zeljko Cecez showing this to you or all three of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All three were showing it like this (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of them ever tell you more precisely what was the fate of Milorad Kuljanin, I mean how and by whom he was shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did. Momir Mrkajic told me the story, who was the best man of Miso Kuljanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that he had been killed by Eso, known as Makaron.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Then let's remain now on this very morning, late morning, when Miso Kuljanin was shot. Did Janko Glogovaz, Momir Mrkajic and Zeljko Cecez have any other occasion to go out of the hangar after this incident the same day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After some time Eso Macic, known as Makaron, and Zenga came through the door and they were looking for three men. They went out. Then they came back shortly afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately at what time of the day did that occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's difficult to tell. Maybe about two hours after this murder. How can I tell the time when I didn't have a watch? I know it was during that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's quite fair, Mr. Dordic. Thank you. So you say these three people remained outside for a very short time. So how long did they stay outside approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About ten minutes on the outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of them say right after entering again into the hangar -- did any of them say what just happened to them outside in those ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I took a risk. I risked being beaten and I went up to Momir Mrkajic, because his sister is my wife, and I asked him: "What did they ask you?" He told me: "They asked us whether we had seen anything." "And what did you say?" "And me and Janko said we hadn't seen anything. Zeljko said that he had seen Eso Macic killing Miso."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Dordic. What happened after that? Did any other incident take place that same day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the evening Zeljko Cecez -- somebody came to the door. It was already dark and we could recognise Zenga by his voice, because he has a specific voice. As soon as we heard his voice, we would try and cover ourselves up, knowing what was going to happen. Then they called him out. He went out, and we could hear terrible blunt blows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean they called out whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zeljko Cecez. He went out and we heard these very hard blunt blows and his moans. This playing with him outside took about almost an hour. We couldn't really tell, but roughly about that long. He was moaning and crying, but they kept on hitting him. At one point the door opened as it was dark. He was probably pushed through the door. We heard him continuing to moan and by his voice we knew that he was moving somehow. He reached his position, the position allotted to him. He started begging for water. He swore at us, asking us to give him water. Not one of the prisoners dared to give him anything, even if they had something to give. After some time these painful moans ceased and in the morning when it dawned I saw him. It was right in front of me that Zeljko Cecez was lying on his stomach. He was barefooted. He had nothing on his legs. He was lying on his stomach. He had a yellow -- the yellow colour of death. I saw that he wasn't moving and I realised that he was dead. We were all shivering with fear. We didn't dare even look, because few of us had contact with dead people. We are afraid of corpses. He lay there in our midst for three or four hours, maybe even longer. Nenad Cecez asked the guards that somebody should come and carry him out and in the morning somewhere around 9 o'clock or 10 o'clock this was done. He was carried out and that was the last time I saw him, when he was carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Dordic, how long could you observe the body remaining motionless in the hangar that morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For about four or five hours at least. I don't know exactly. As again, I said no watch, but it was a long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you observe personally that during that time the body didn't have any movement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is what he has already said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is what he has already said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did anybody order to remove the body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Hazim Delic came and ordered Nenad Cecez and some others to carry him out, and they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the last time that you saw the body of this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you personally observe any other incident which led to the death of a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were quite a few such cases. The next case was with Scepo Gotovac. This Scepo Gotovac was an elderly man, around 70 years old, maybe even older.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Dordic. Can you say approximately when did this incident happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think some time in June, end of June. I think that's where it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you go ahead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Scepo Gotovac was right next to the door and during the day Hazim Delic came in. He carried a piece of paper in his hand. He told Scepo Gotovac to get up and he did. Hazim started reading something to the effect that Scepo Gotovac some time in November 1942 or 1943 -- I don't know exactly -- at that same spot right where this hangar was, at that spot that he had killed two Muslims and that he was going to finish at the same spot. He begged him and he swore that he didn't do that, but this one did not believe it. So he started beating him. Then he was taken out. That is Delic took him outside. Outside blunt blows could be heard and that went on for about half an hour, maybe even longer. He kept moaning. We kept hearing these blunt blows. At one point he -- the door opened and he was pushed inside, inside the hangar. He lay down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Did you see who put him inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He entered on all fours. He lay there practically immobile and moaning and then during the evening -- I know by the voice, because I heard it -- I heard that Landzo came to the door. He opened the door and he called Scepo out. He said: "Scepo, come out", and he said: "I can't. Kill me here." Then he ordered some prisoners to carry him out. I think Novo Zelenovic and another one carried him out because Novo Zelenovic was right there at the door. Again we could hear terrible blows, his moans, and after a while these moans stopped. We heard the door open and these two -- Zenga called out these two prisoners to carry him in. They did that. He ordered -- at that time he ordered that nobody could take off something that was on his forehead, but we didn't know what it was. In the morning he lay there motionless. He was all yellowish and black and blue. He had a badge on. I think it was either an SDS badge or something. I don't know. It was pinned to his forehead or nailed to his forehead. I went out to urinate and I saw him. I was about 1 metre away from him. This body was left there for two or three hours and then Nenad Cecez again called the guards to have him removed, and then he was removed and that is the last that I saw of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, what was the position inside the hangar where Gotovac used to sit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right next to the door. He was the first one going up from the door to the right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you could see his body going the next morning outside to urinate; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you observe the body in this occasion with some care? Can you describe it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Black and blue and also yellowish, as a dead man, and he lay motionless.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the time when you could see something on your forehead (sic)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a badge of some sort. I think it was an SDS badge. That would be the Serbian Democratic Party badge. It was like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Besides the chance you had to see him from a very close position going outside to urinate, did you have a chance to observe the body from your position while you were sitting in your position in the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you observe the body remaining motionless for a significant time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long could you observe the body remaining motionless in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two or three hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say at what time was the body removed approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere around 8 o'clock at the latest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody order to remove the body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Delic came and some guards and they ordered it to be carried out after the request of Nenad Cecez, because if you were to request something of the guards, from the guards, that would all go through Nenad Cecez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was the last time you saw the body of this person; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Could you personally observe any other incident which led to the death of a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just two or three days after the murder of Scepo Gotovac we heard some screams outside, and we knew that somebody came in, but didn't know who it was. Only in the morning we saw, and I knew this Nedjo Milosevic personally. He sat almost at the same spot where Scepo Gotovac used to sit. I saw him all black and blue, beaten up, and he lay there nearly motionless. He spent the whole day there and in the evening hours Zenga opened the door came to Nedjo and said: "Nedjo, come on out." Nedjo said he couldn't. Then Zenga ordered two prisoners to carry him out, which they did. Outside a terrible beating started. We heard blows, his moans, and after about 20 minutes or half an hour, it all stopped. He fell silent and the door never opened. I don't know what happened to him. He was probably killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any other incident you could personally observe which led to the death of a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Simo Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you approximately say when did this incident happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometime at the end of June or early July, around them. Simo Jovanovic had been taken out in the evening several times. Usually it was a neighbour of his, who was from the same village that he was from. I think his name was Adam Cosic. For the most part Zenga was also with him. This Cosic would say: "Come on, neighbour. I have something to tell you." Then he would come out and then you could hear terrible blows outside. He would be moaning and then after a while he would be brought back in. This happened several times over a period of about ten days. Then on one occasion the door opened and Adem Cosic walked in, came pretty close to Simo, and Zenga stood at the door, and he said: "Simo, come on out." Simo somehow got out. We could hear blunt blows, his moans, and after a while the door opened again. Apparently he was ordered to come back in and Simo somehow came in, came to his place. It was already dark by that time. We could not see how he was walking. We heard -- we knew approximately where his spot was. We could hear those painful grunts and moans and he asked for help. After a while everything became quiet and in the morning, when it dawned, we saw Simo lying motionless. We realised that he was dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, focusing on the last time Simo Jovanovic was called out of the hangar on the last evening, can you say approximately at what time he was called outside that last occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the early dusk. I don't know what time. Around 9.00, maybe even earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he, Simo Jovanovic, came back into the hangar after this last occasion and reached his position inside the hangar, can you say where was his position inside the hangar with respect to your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Like this (indicating). I was here and he was around here somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could tell us in terms of how many metres approximately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If the hangar was 25 metres long, he could have been 10-12 metres away from me, somewhere midway, maybe a bit further away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was a time that night or in the morning when you could observe clearly Mr. Jovanovic or his body with some attention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that? In the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the morning, when it dawned, around 5 o'clock, maybe even before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe the body as you could see it from your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
